verses.translation_literal: A maskil of Asaph. Give ear, my people, [to] my torah; incline your ear to the sayings of my mouth.
verses.translation_dramatic: A teaching song, by Asaph. Listen, my people. Lean in. This is my teaching, the words of my own mouth, and you must bend your ear to catch every one.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the voice of a teacher stepping to the front of a gathered crowd, probably at a festival at the sanctuary; the opening is the call of a wisdom teacher, not a priest reading statute. The speaker calls the audience 'my people' and the speech 'my torah', which means 'instruction' in the sense of a parent's or teacher's teaching (compare Prov 1:8). The KJV and ASV say 'law', which makes it sound like a legal code; what follows is a long recited history, and the Hebrew word covers that. Malbim goes further: for him the telling of Israel's past is itself torah, and the story's outer shell ('the words of my mouth') is bound up with the teaching inside it. The KJV also leaves 'Maschil' as an untranslated label; it marks an artful, instructive poem. Notice the sound-play: the verb 'give ear' (ha'azinah) is built from the noun for ear ('ozen), and the ear comes again in 'incline your ear' (oznekhem). The ear is everywhere in this line. Actors: this is an order, delivered warmly. An ancient audience could not read a text; everything depended on what entered the ear.

philological_notes.note: A heading used for a number of psalms, usually taken to mean an instructive or skillfully made poem (from the root 'to be prudent, to have insight'). Its exact sense is not settled. Ibn Ezra takes it as a piyyut whose opening word gives the genre, a label, not a command.
From the root 'to throw, to point, to teach'. Here 'instruction', not statute: Radak says it is what the speaker teaches in recounting God's goodness to Israel; Malbim says the story itself is torah.
A verb made from the noun 'ear' ('ozen), literally 'to ear', so 'give ear'. The echo with 'your ear' ('oznekhem) two words later is audible in Hebrew.

verses.translation_literal: I will open my mouth in a parable; I will pour out riddles from of old.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will open my mouth, and a parable will come. Then riddles, poured out like water from a spring, riddles older than any of us can remember.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker promises two kinds of speech, a mashal and chidot. A mashal is a comparison, a proverb or a pointed story; a chidah is a riddle, a saying whose sense must be worked out. The commentators ask what the riddles are, and they give different answers. Radak points to two puzzling phrases inside the psalm. 'Bread of the mighty' (v. 25) is the manna, spoken of as a riddle; 'he gave his might into captivity' (v. 61) is the ark, and Radak adds that no one could have understood that line had 1 Samuel not told of the ark's capture. Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra stress the ark example in the same way. Rashi takes 'parable' more broadly, as the words of Torah themselves. Malbim reads the verse as a boast: the other peoples had myths of their gods, invented stories whose meaning only the priests knew, but Israel's riddles are things 'we have heard and known', handed down by fathers who say they truly happened. The KJV 'dark sayings' is a respectable attempt, but the Hebrew word is plainly 'riddles', the word used of Samson's riddle in Judges 14. The verb 'pour out' (abbi'ah) is a spring image: speech welling up like water from a source. The KJV flattens it to 'utter'. 'From of old' (mini-qedem) says the riddles come from antiquity. Matthew 13:35 later quotes this verse, but the psalm itself is about telling Israel's story.

philological_notes.note: 'I will gush forth, pour out', a spring image (nova' is a bubbling spring). Metzudat Zion links it to Ps 19:3, 'day to day pours out speech'.

Riddles, enigmatic sayings; the same word as Samson's riddle. Radak says a chidah is a hidden or obscure matter; for him the manna ('bread of the mighty') and, separately, the ark taken captive (understood only from 1 Samuel) are the examples. Metzudat David gives the ark example.

verses.translation_literal: Which we have heard, and we know them, and our fathers have recounted to us.
verses.translation_dramatic: These are things we heard, and in the hearing came to know them; things our fathers told us, one night after another by the fire.
verses.directors_commentary: The chain of transmission is the point. 'Heard', 'known' and 'recounted' are three links: what the fathers say, what the children take in, what they now claim as their own knowledge. In Hebrew 'know' (yada') is not mere information but intimacy, knowing a thing by living with it. The KJV, 'heard and known', keeps this; the BBE blurs it into 'come to our hearing and our knowledge'. What the KJV cannot show is the Hebrew's change of tense: 'we have heard' is completed, 'we have known them' continues as a state, and 'recounted' is again complete. For an audience without books, a father's word carried the weight of testimony. Radak and Metzudat David both say the point is that no father would plant a false story in his son's heart, which is why the claim of truth rests on family trust.

philological_notes.note: 'They recounted', the same root as 'scribe' and 'book' (sefer), but here an oral telling, in the piel (an intensive 'to relate in detail'). The root returns in verse 4 ('recounting') and verse 6 ('may they recount'), so the psalm is a chain of tellings.

verses.translation_literal: We will not hide [them] from their children, to a later generation recounting the praises of YHWH, and his might, and his wonders which he has done.
verses.translation_dramatic: We will not hide them from their children. We will tell the next generation, and the one that follows, the praises of the LORD, his strength, and the wonders he has done.
verses.directors_commentary: A vow made on behalf of the whole community. 'Hide' (kachad) is a strong word for withholding, as in 1 Samuel 3:18, where Samuel 'hid nothing' from Eli; silence about God would be a kind of theft from the children. Who are 'their children'? Radak says: the children of our fathers, our brothers in Israel who never learned the tradition, and those of us who know it are bound to tell them so that they too will tell their children, down to the last generation. The KJV 'shewing' for 'recounting' smooths a repeated verb: the same root (sapar) that brought the story from the fathers in verse 3 now carries it forward, so the chain is visible only in Hebrew. 'Praises' (tehillot) is the word that names the whole book of Psalms. 'Might' ('uzzo, from 'oz) and 'wonders' (nifla'ot) are what Israel's story is about: God's power and his astonishing acts. Malbim alone sets this against the myths of the Greeks: those are kept back from children and handed only to elders and priests, and they tell of the gods' faults, their weakness and wonders that never happened, whereas Israel tells God's praises, his might and the wonders he really did.

philological_notes.note: 'We will hide, withhold'. Metzudat Zion links it to 1 Sam 3:18 ('he did not hide it from him'): the sense is deliberate concealment.
'His wonders', things beyond ordinary human power. The same root as pele' in verse 12, which makes the opening and the first historical example rhyme.

verses.translation_literal: And he raised up a testimony in Jacob, and a torah he set in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, to make them known to their children.
verses.translation_dramatic: For he raised up a witness in Jacob and set down a teaching in Israel, and he commanded our fathers to make it known to their children.
verses.directors_commentary: Two nouns, 'testimony' and 'torah', and two verbs for putting them in place: 'he raised up' (wayyaqem) and 'he set' (sam). 'Testimony' ('edut) is the witness-document: the same word used for the tablets in the ark, the 'ark of the testimony'. 'Jacob' and 'Israel' are the same man and the same people, but poetry spreads them across the two lines as a parallel, and neither the KJV nor the BBE needs to read them as two groups. The KJV 'appointed a law' misses that 'set' (sam) is the ordinary verb for placing something where it will stand. The commandment itself is the crux: God did not only give the law, he commanded the fathers to teach it. 'To make known' (lehodi'am) is the causative of 'know' in verse 3: the chain of knowledge is a commanded duty (compare Deut 6:7, 'you shall teach them diligently to your children'). Malbim reads 'testimony' as the plain stories and 'torah' as the teachings that come out of them; Ibn Ezra reads 'testimony' as the commandments that reason itself bears witness to.

philological_notes.note: 'Testimony, witness', here what God's act put on record. Meiri compares it with Ps 19:8 ('the testimony of the LORD is sure'), where it names the portion of faith that bears witness.
'To make them known', the causative form of the verb 'to know' used in verse 3 ('we know them'). What was known by hearing is now to be made known to others.

verses.translation_literal: So that a later generation may know, children who will be born; they will arise and recount [them] to their children.
verses.translation_dramatic: So that the generation still to come might know it, the children not yet born, and that they too would rise up and tell their own children.
verses.directors_commentary: The chain now stretches into the future, and the verbs of the passage sound like a relay race: 'know', 'be born', 'arise', 'recount'. 'Arise' (yaqumu) rhymes with 'he raised up' (wayyaqem) in verse 5: God raises up a witness, and each new generation must itself rise up and take it over. The KJV hedges with 'should be born' and 'should arise', as if it were a hope in the conditional mood; the Hebrew imperfect is open, and the final verb is a wish ('may they recount') or a purpose. The BBE's 'children of the future' is clear but misses the Hebrew's neat doubling of 'children' (banim) and 'their children' (benehem), which is the real idea: a family tree of tellers. Nothing here is dramatic yet; the scene is a long breath before the story begins. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David both stress that the chain is to run to the end of time.

philological_notes.note: 'They will arise', the same root as 'he raised up' in verse 5; each generation takes its turn standing up to tell.

verses.translation_literal: And they will put in God their confidence, and not forget the deeds of God, and his commandments they will keep.
verses.translation_dramatic: That they might set their trust in God, and never forget what God has done, and keep his commandments.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the purpose of all the telling is stated plainly: trust, memory and obedience. The Hebrew phrases are physical: 'put their confidence in God' is literally to place something, and the thing placed is 'kesel', a word whose root meaning is the loins or flank, the part of the body that carries the weight; 'confidence' here means what you lean on. The KJV 'hope' is not wrong, but it makes the word sound softer than it is: it is trust, the thing you put your whole weight on (compare Job 31:24, 'gold my confidence'). Memory and obedience come as a pair: to forget God's deeds is to stop keeping his commands. The KJV 'works of God' softens ma'alelei-El, 'the deeds of God': the noun comes from the root of 'to act', and in the Psalms it often has a flavor of deliberate acts of judgment or deliverance. Ibn Ezra's reading is a sequence: when they do not forget, then they will keep.

philological_notes.note: 'Their confidence'. Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all gloss it as trust or hope; Rashi and Metzudat Zion cite Job 31:24 ('If I have made gold my confidence').
'Deeds', a word for what someone has done, sometimes with a sense of an act with consequences. It leads to the 'deeds' (alilot) of verse 11, where the same family reappears as what Israel forgot.

verses.translation_literal: And they will not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation, a generation that did not make firm its heart, and whose spirit was not faithful with God.
verses.translation_dramatic: And may they not be like their fathers: a stubborn, rebellious generation, a generation whose heart was never set firm, and whose spirit would not hold faith with God.
verses.directors_commentary: The tone turns. The warning against the 'fathers' is a deliberate echo of the 'stubborn and rebellious son' of Deuteronomy 21:18, the son who will not obey his parents: 'sorer' and 'moreh' are those very two words. Here a whole generation is cast as that son, and the audience hears the family language: the God of Israel is the father who was defied. The KJV 'set not their heart aright' is smoother than the Hebrew, 'did not make firm its heart' (lo' hekhin libbo): the verb kun means to establish, to make solid, to fix in place, so the picture is a heart that never stood on a firm base. 'Stedfast' for ne'emnah is the passive of the root of 'amen' and 'faith'; the spirit was not made trustworthy. The repeated 'generation' is a heavy drumbeat. For Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David the fathers are the wilderness generation; Malbim reads the passage as a charge against the whole line that came before David.

philological_notes.note: 'Stubborn and rebellious', the same pair as the 'stubborn and rebellious son' of Deut 21:18, 20. Metzudat Zion glosses the first as turning away from the right path and the second as rebelling and refusing.

'Set its heart firm'. The verb means to fix, establish, or prepare; the heart is imagined as something that needs a foundation. Metzudat David says: it did not direct its heart toward the word of the LORD.

verses.translation_literal: The sons of Ephraim, equipped, shooters of the bow, turned [back] on the day of battle.
verses.translation_dramatic: The sons of Ephraim: armed to the teeth, drawing their bows. And on the day of battle they turned, and they ran.
verses.directors_commentary: The first concrete case, and a baffling one, which even the old commentators did not agree about. Ephraim is the leading tribe of the northern kingdom and its name can stand for all Israel; at Shiloh, in Ephraim's land, the tabernacle once stood. A bow was the weapon of the professional soldier, so the line sets up the surprise: the best-armed fighters were the ones who turned. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David link the line to 1 Chronicles 7:21, where Ephraimites raided Gath and were killed, or to an early, unauthorized exit from Egypt; Ibn Ezra and Malbim think of a defeat at Shiloh, with the Philistines in the time of Eli. The psalm itself gives no name, which is part of its method: the story is told as a riddle, as verse 2 promised. The KJV 'being armed, and carrying bows' turns a Hebrew chain of two nouns into two clauses and adds 'back' after 'turned', although Hebrew has just 'they turned'. 'Day of battle' (yom qerav) is the Hebrew idiom for the decisive hour. Director: do not play this as cowardice, but as a collapse of confidence that no weapon could prevent.

philological_notes.note: A chain of two participles: 'equipped, shooters of the bow'. Metzudat Zion glosses nosheqei as 'armed' (compare 2 Chr 17:17) and romei as 'throwing, shooting' (compare Jer 4:29, 'the sound of the horseman and the bowshooter'); Rashi links romei to Ex 15:1 ('he has thrown into the sea'). Radak reads the chain as 'armed, and shooters of the bow'.
'They turned', with no object. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David take it as 'turned the neck/back', a retreat.

verses.translation_literal: They did not keep the covenant of God, and in his torah they refused to walk.
verses.translation_dramatic: They did not keep God's covenant. When it came to walking in his teaching, they refused.
verses.directors_commentary: The reason for the defeat is given at once, and it has nothing to do with weapons. A covenant is a treaty between a great king and a people, and 'keeping' (shamar) it means guarding it as a sentry guards a wall. The refusal is physical: 'they refused to walk'. In the Hebrew world, 'walk' is the standard word for how a life is lived, and 'ma'anu' (they refused) is the verb of the stubborn child. The KJV 'refused to walk in his law' is accurate here, though it again turns torah into 'law'. Ibn Ezra and Radak say the covenant is the one made at Sinai. Notice the word order: 'in his torah they refused to walk', with the refused thing in front for stress.

philological_notes.note: 'They refused', a verb of flat, obstinate refusal; Metzudat Zion glosses it simply 'they did not want'. It is the verb used of Pharaoh's refusals in Exodus.

verses.translation_literal: And they forgot his deeds, and his wonders which he had shown them.
verses.translation_dramatic: They forgot what he had done, and the wonders he had made them see.
verses.directors_commentary: The first failure was not an act but a lapse of memory, the sin the whole opening of the psalm fears. 'Forget' (shakhach) in Hebrew means more than an absent mind; it means that memory has stopped governing action. The KJV 'forgat' is archaic. 'Deeds' ('alilot) is a stronger word than 'works': it names deliberate acts, often with moral weight, and it is the cousin of 'deeds' in verse 7. 'Which he had shown them' is the Hebrew hiphil of 'see': God made them see. The verb is causative, so the wonders were not hidden, they were put before the eyes of those who forgot. Ibn Ezra notes that the same wonders are said to be 'hidden' (nifla'ot) and shown (her'am): wonders are 'hidden' because beyond understanding, yet God made them seen. The verse is the hinge between the opening vow (do not forget) and the history: the story that follows is the list of what was forgotten.

philological_notes.note: 'His deeds', a word for deliberate acts; related to ma'alelei in verse 7.
'He made them see' (hiphil). Ibn Ezra points out the contrast between 'wonders' (hidden, beyond understanding) and 'he showed them'.

verses.translation_literal: Before their fathers he did a wonder, in the land of Egypt, the field of Zoan.
verses.translation_dramatic: In front of their fathers he did a wonder, in the land of Egypt, in the open country of Zoan.
verses.directors_commentary: The history proper begins, and it begins at the center of the enemy's power. Zoan (Tanis) lay in the eastern Nile Delta; it was a royal city of Egypt, close to the old Ramesside capital, so the wonders were done almost at the door of Pharaoh's court. The place name is the answer to the question of who stood to see them: the whole Delta. 'Before their fathers' (neged avotam) is more vivid than the KJV 'in the sight of': neged means 'in front of, opposite', face to face, a witness at close range. The Hebrew has a singular, 'a wonder' (pele'), where the KJV has plural 'marvellous things'; Radak says the singular is a general term for many wonders. 'Field of Zoan' (sedeh-tso'an) and 'land of Egypt' are a pair in parallel: 'sedeh' here means region, as in 'the field of Moab' (Ruth 1:1). Rashi and Metzudat David bring a midrash that has the patriarchs themselves see, at the sea, how God redeems their children.

philological_notes.note: 'A wonder', a singular, a general word for the whole set of miracles. Radak says it is a collective: not one wonder but many.
'The field/country of Zoan'. Radak and Metzudat David read it as a parallel to 'land of Egypt', with Zoan as a royal city of Egypt; Ibn Ezra compares 'the field of Edom'.
'In front of, in the sight of'. Malbim reads it as 'before their eyes'; Radak reads the 'fathers' as the witnesses whose children later heard of it and did not see.

verses.translation_literal: He split [the] sea and he brought them across, and he made waters stand like a heap.
verses.translation_dramatic: He split the sea open, and through the opening he led them over, and the waters he raised and held upright, standing like a heaped mound.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three verbs in a row, each with the same subject and no pause: split, bring across, make stand. Play it as one unbroken motion, with the weight on the last, because the sea does not merely part, it is set on its feet. The verb ויצב is a causative (Hiphil) of נצב, 'to stand': God stands the water up the way a soldier is stood at a post.

KJV 'divided' is gentler than בָּקַע, which is the verb for cleaving wood, ripping open a belly or breaking open the ground; the sea is torn, not parted like curtains. KJV 'caused them to pass through' is fair, but the Hebrew has the plain 'brought them across', the same verb (עבר) that Psalm 78 uses elsewhere of crossing a boundary. KJV 'an heap' is right, and it is worth keeping the oddness: נֵד is a rare word for a mound or dam of piled water, found in the Song of the Sea (Exod 15:8), the crossing of the Jordan (Josh 3:13, 16), Isa 17:11 and Ps 33:7. Here the psalmist is quoting the Exodus language on purpose, so that listeners who know the Song of the Sea hear it behind the verse. For a nomadic or farming audience, a heap is grain on a threshing floor or earth in a rampart: something solid that holds its shape. The line also has no article before 'sea' and 'waters', so it reads like a headline of the event rather than a described scene.

philological_notes.note: To cleave, split open by force; used of splitting wood, breaking open the ground and tearing open the sea. It is stronger than a neutral 'divide'. The verb is a perfect, but in this psalm's recital it carries the tone of narrative past.

A heap or mound, here of water. Rashi explains it as a high mound (תל גבוה) and cites the Targum of Exod 15:8, 'they stood like a wall'; Radak and Metzudat Zion point back to Exod 15:8. The word recurs rarely, which makes the borrowing from the Song of the Sea audible.

verses.translation_literal: And he led them with the cloud by day, and all the night with a light of fire.
verses.translation_dramatic: By day he led them under a cloud, a canopy of shade over the glare of the wilderness; and all through the night, by the glow of fire.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the violence of the sea, the tempo drops. Two short halves set day against night, and the second half stretches: 'and all the night' is the longest stretch of the line, so let it slow and run on. The verb וינחם is a gentle, shepherd-like word for guiding along a road (cf. Ps 23:3), where KJV 'led' is accurate but loses the care. Note too that the Hebrew has 'the cloud', with the article, as a known thing the audience has heard of.

In a hot desert, shade by day and light at night are not marvels for the eye only; they are protection from the sun and from the cold, dark and predators of the night. Ibn Ezra reads it as kindness: the cloud kept the sun off them, and the fire meant they needed no torches. KJV 'in the daytime also' adds 'also' that the Hebrew does not have, and ASV and Webster keep it; YLT and BBE are closer. The 'light of fire' (אור אש) is an unusual phrase, and no pillar is named in the verse itself, though Radak and Malbim understand the pillars of cloud and fire of Exod 13:21 behind it.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of נחה, 'to lead, guide'; a verb of a shepherd or guide, rather than a general's 'command'. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'he drove/guided them' (נהגם).
'Light of fire', that is, firelight, not a flame as such. Radak reads it as the fire that lasted all night until daybreak, so that they needed no night lamp.

verses.translation_literal: He splits rocks in the wilderness, and gave drink like deeps, abundant.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the wilderness he broke the rocks open, and gave them drink: drink as if from the great deep itself, welling up without end.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the sea to the desert. The first verb is the same 'split' as in v. 13: the Lord who cleaves the sea cleaves the stone. Let the actor feel the echo.

The Hebrew changes tense in mid-line: 'he splits' (an imperfect, as if it were still going on) and then 'and he gave drink' (a narrative form). Radak says the imperfect stands for the past (on Psalm 78:15). The KJV smooths it into one past tense and so loses the sense of a habit repeated again and again. 'Rocks' is plural, and Radak places the events at Rephidim and Kadesh, two separate rocks; Rashi cites Exodus 17:6 for the first. The simile is startling: not 'as from a spring' but 'like deeps' (תהומות), the primeval ocean under the earth of Genesis 1:2, the water that no desert should have. The adjective 'abundant' is feminine singular after a plural noun, which Ibn Ezra and Radak explain as a poetic variation (on Psalm 78:15). The KJV 'great depths' captures it, though the Hebrew word is just 'much'.

philological_notes.note: 'Like deeps': the same word as the primeval deep of Genesis 1:2. The simile gives the wilderness water cosmic abundance. Rashi (on Psalm 78:15) adds that even at the sea the waters beneath were turned sweet.
Rocks, in the plural, unlike the singular rock of v. 16 and v. 20. Radak says two events are meant, Rephidim and Kadesh; Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'rocks' (סלעים).

verses.translation_literal: And he brought out streams from a rock, and made water go down like rivers.
verses.translation_dramatic: Streams came out of the rock, out of stone that had held nothing but dust, and he sent the water down the slope like rivers, running, running.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the answer to the previous line, in different words, which is how Hebrew poetry works: Radak says it 'doubles the matter with other words' (on Psalm 78:16). Play it as a rising, a gathering of speed.

Two verbs, both of motion: 'brought out' and 'made go down'. Radak notes that the second is apt because the rock is a high place, so the water literally descends. 'Streams' (נוזלים) are trickles, flowing liquid, from a verb for dripping and flowing (Metzudat Zion), and the simile jumps to 'rivers' (נהרות), the great perennial waters that a desert people could only dream of. The KJV is faithful here, and even adds an 'also' that is not in the Hebrew. Rashi reads the rivers as a tradition from the well that followed Israel, with the princes tracing channels with their staffs to each tribe's camp (citing Numbers 21:18); that is a later midrash and not in the verse.

philological_notes.note: Flowing things, streams or trickles: a participle from the verb of dripping and flowing, used for water running down. Metzudat Zion ties it to dripping and flowing.

verses.translation_literal: And they went on again to sin against him, to rebel against Most High in the dry land.
verses.translation_dramatic: And still they sinned against him. More, again. In the dry country, with the water not yet dry on their lips, they defied the Most High.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn. Everything so far has been gift, and here the voice drops and hardens. The audience should feel the ingratitude as a physical thing: the same people, the same desert, the same water.

The verb 'went on' (ויוסיפו) is literally 'they added', and with 'again' the Hebrew piles on the repetition; the psalm will say this over and over. The KJV 'provoking' is a decent translation of 'to rebel' (מרות), but it understates it: Rashi glosses 'to anger' and cites Deuteronomy 9:7, while Metzudat Zion says 'to rebel'; the root is the one for rebelliousness. 'The Most High' (עליון) is a title for God above all other powers, and Malbim hears the sin as precisely a denial that the God of Israel is that Most High, a God who could rule even over the dry land (on Psalm 78:17). 'In the dry land' (בציה) is a word for parched, waterless country: Ibn Ezra stresses the irony that they rebelled against him in the very place where they most needed him.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive of the hiphil of מרה, 'to rebel, to be defiant'. Rashi glosses 'to provoke', Metzudat Zion 'to rebel'; Radak says it stands for להמרות.
'Most High': a title of God as supreme over everything; Radak says it is used because everything is in his hand, including bringing water from rock and, later, meat.

verses.translation_literal: And they tested God in their heart, by asking food for their throat.
verses.translation_dramatic: They put God to the test, there in their hearts, and asked for food, food to feed their own hunger and their own craving.
verses.directors_commentary:
The sin is made precise: not hunger but a test. Give it a hushed, inward reading, because the verse says it all happens 'in their heart', before a word is spoken.

'Tested' (נסה) is the verb for putting something to the proof to see if it will break, and it is used elsewhere of the people at Massah. The KJV 'tempted' is an archaism that now means seduce; the Hebrew means 'put to the test', as in modern 'try God'. The prepositional phrase 'in their heart' matters: Radak (on Psalm 78:18) says the test was in their thoughts, because the manna was already good and they did not need the meat, but they said aloud that they did. Metzudat David says the same. The last word is נֶפֶשׁ, which the KJV renders 'lust'; it is the word for the throat, the self, the appetite, and 'for their lust' is stronger than the Hebrew, which says 'for their own selves'. Radak glosses it 'for their desire', the nefesh being the seat of craving. ASV and Webster say 'desire', which is closer. I keep 'throat' in the literal layer to show the bodily sense.

philological_notes.note: Throat, appetite, self: the seat of craving. Radak (on Psalm 78:18) glosses it as desire, since the nefesh is the 'owner of desire'. KJV 'lust' over-moralizes.
They tested, put to the proof. The test is inward ('in their heart'); Radak and Metzudat David say the test was in their intentions rather than in what they said.

verses.translation_literal: And they spoke against God, they said, 'Is God able to arrange a table in the wilderness?'
verses.translation_dramatic: They spoke against God. They said it aloud: 'Can God lay a table here, in the wilderness?'
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the heart's test comes out of the mouth. The actors should say the question with a sneer that is also, underneath, real fear.

The Hebrew has a pair of verbs, 'they spoke against' and 'they said', which gives the quotation weight. 'Against' is a hostile use of the preposition (ב). The KJV 'furnish' is a stately word, but the Hebrew verb (ערך) is to set in order or lay out, as for battle or for a meal. The 'table' (שלחן) is the picture of a full meal, and Ibn Ezra reads it as a figure for meat (on Psalm 78:19). The question starts with an interrogative particle plus 'is he able' and the divine name used is the generic אֵל, not YHWH, which makes the insult cooler and more distant. Radak points out the wilderness is a place where nothing living can be found (on Psalm 78:19); the table is a luxury.

philological_notes.note: A table: originally the leather mat or spread laid on the ground for a meal. It stands for a full meal; Ibn Ezra reads it as a figure for meat.
To arrange, set in order. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'arrangement'.

verses.translation_literal: Look! He struck a rock and waters flowed out, and torrents overflowed. Is he also able to give bread, or will he prepare meat for his people?
verses.translation_dramatic: 'Yes, look: he struck the rock, and water poured out, and torrents ran over. But bread, too? Can he give bread? Will he set out meat for his own people?'
verses.directors_commentary:
The quotation continues, and it is a grudging concession followed by a dare. The speakers admit the miracle, and use it as the ground of the next demand. Deliver it fast, with a mocking kind of reasoning.

The opening 'Look!' (הן) points at the evidence. Two verbs of violence and plenty: 'struck' (הכה) and 'flowed out' (זוב, the word used of a spring or of a body's flow), then 'torrents' (נחלים) that 'overflow' (שטף), a word for flood. The question is double: 'bread' and 'meat'. The KJV 'flesh' is accurate for שְׁאֵר (Rashi glosses it as בשר, and Metzudat Zion cites Micah 3:3), but the point is that 'bread' (לחם) may itself mean meat: Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all cite 'my food, my offering' (Numbers 28:2), where 'bread' is a sacrifice. So the second half may just repeat the first, as Radak says it does, 'doubling the matter in other words'. There is a real puzzle here for readers of the Torah: Ibn Ezra notes that the manna came before the rock at Rephidim (Exodus 16 and 17), and he and Radak both try to resolve it. For the performance, you need only the tone: they are testing him. Radak says (on Psalm 78:20) that this was all in their hearts, not spoken aloud.

philological_notes.note: Flesh, meat; a poetic parallel to 'bread'. Rashi glosses it בשר; Metzudat Zion cites Micah 3:3 ('who eat the flesh of my people').

Bread, food; in this line the commentators read it as meat, as 'my food' is used of offerings in Numbers 28:2. Meiri also notes that the particle ה in הגם is the emphatic interrogative, as in 1 Samuel 2:27.
Wadis or torrents: dry channels that run only in flood. Radak says the water came out so abundantly that great torrents flooded the land.

verses.translation_literal: Therefore YHWH heard and was furious, and fire was kindled in Jacob, and also anger went up in Israel.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD heard. He heard every word, and fury swept over him. Fire was kindled among Jacob's children, and anger went up against Israel, rising like smoke.
verses.directors_commentary:
The cloud darkens. The earlier lines spoke of the Lord's care, and here the speaker's voice turns cold; the pause before 'heard' is the whole drama.

'Heard' is the verb of a reaction, not just of hearing: Meiri and Radak read it as God taking note of what was said, even what was only in the heart (Radak on Psalm 78:21). The verb 'was furious' (ויתעבר) is from the root 'to cross over, overflow', and in the reflexive form means to burst the bank of one's anger, like a river in flood, which links back to the torrents of v. 20. The KJV 'wroth' is archaic but fair. 'Fire was kindled' uses a rare verb for lighting a fire (נשקה): Rashi links it to Ezekiel 39:9 ('they will light and burn'), and to Numbers 11:1, where fire from the LORD burned at the edge of the camp. The KJV adds 'against' where the Hebrew has the preposition 'in': the fire is kindled in Jacob, in the midst of the people. 'Jacob' and 'Israel' are the same people under their two names; Radak calls it the same thing said twice in different words, while Malbim distinguishes the lower and higher ranks (on Psalm 78:21). Radak also ties the verse to two events, Taberah (Numbers 11:1-3) and Kibroth-hattaavah (Numbers 11:31-34).

philological_notes.note: Reflexive of 'to cross over': to overflow, to burst out in rage. Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion gloss it as being filled with wrath.
A rare verb for kindling or stoking a fire. Rashi links it to הִשִּׂיקוּ in Ezekiel 39:9 and to Numbers 11:1; Metzudat Zion glosses it as burning.

verses.translation_literal: For they did not believe in God, and they did not trust in his salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: For they had not believed in God. They had not trusted him to save them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verdict, given flatly. The psalm does not say they were greedy or loud; it says they did not trust. Play it plain and unadorned, after the fire of the last verse.

The verse is a matched pair, 'not believed' and 'not trusted', which Ibn Ezra calls a doubled sense (on Psalm 78:22). The first verb is the hiphil of אמן, the root of 'amen' and of firmness, so it means to rest one's weight on something, which is why the KJV 'believed not in God' is close but a little abstract. The second (בטח) is the word for secure reliance, to lean on. 'His salvation' (ישועה) is deliverance, rescue, and Radak says they failed to trust that he who had saved them many times could bring them into the land. Metzudat David says they did not believe he could fulfil their requests. The KJV and ASV reproduce the 'not' twice and are faithful here.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of the root of 'amen': to rely on as firm. Radak (on Psalm 78:22) says they did not believe he could bring them into the land.
To trust, to lean securely. The two verbs are a doubled statement, per Ibn Ezra.

verses.translation_literal: And he commanded skies from above, and doors of heaven he opened.
verses.translation_dramatic: Yet he spoke a word to the skies above, and opened the doors of heaven.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mercy that follows the rage, and the first note is wonder. Let the voice lift upward: the camera goes up into the sky.

The verse uses a different word for the sky from the usual: 'skies' (שחקים), the thin upper layer of cloud, the dust of the heavens, set against 'heaven' (שמים) in the next line. Malbim (on Psalm 78:23) makes a point of the difference: the 'skies' are higher than the heavens, and mark the miraculous rather than the natural supply. The 'doors of heaven' are an old image of rain falling through windows or gates in the sky dome, as in the Flood story. The KJV and Webster 'Though he had commanded' turn the narrative verbs into a concessive pluperfect: Ibn Ezra reads 'and he had commanded' (on Psalm 78:23), and Radak says he had already commanded them to give manna. The Hebrew itself has a plain past, and the sequence of 'Therefore the fire' (v. 21) and now 'he commanded' sets two answers side by side: punishment and provision. The 'Though' is an interpretation and is a good guess, not a translation.

philological_notes.note: The skies, a poetic word for the upper heavens or cloud layer: literally the thin or dusty stuff. Malbim distinguishes it from 'heaven' as higher and marking miraculous supply.
The doors of heaven: the sky as a building with doors through which rain, here manna, comes. Radak says it signifies the abundance of manna.

verses.translation_literal: And he rained on them manna to eat, and grain of heaven he gave to them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he rained manna down on them to eat. Grain from heaven he gave them, bread from the sky.
verses.directors_commentary:
The windows open and the food falls. Keep the cadence unhurried and full: this is the gift they did not ask for in this form.

'Rained' (וימטר) is the verb of rain, so manna falls like weather. 'Manna' (מן) is the name given in Exodus 16, which explains it as a question, 'what is it?'; the psalm gives it two names, 'manna' and 'grain of heaven', as Metzudat David notes, the second a doubling of the first. The KJV 'corn of heaven' is a trap: 'corn' in older English means grain, any cereal, and a modern reader pictures maize. The Hebrew דגן is the staple cereal, wheat or barley, so 'grain' is right. Radak says the manna was in place of grain and better. As with v. 23, the KJV and Webster use the pluperfect ('had rained'), following Ibn Ezra who argues the sense is 'he had already rained' (on Psalm 78:24); the Hebrew has simple past forms, and the order of manna and rock in the Torah (Exodus 16 before Exodus 17) is exactly the puzzle he addresses. Metzudat David too: 'he had already rained the manna, and so they saw that his hand is not short.'

philological_notes.note: 'Grain of heaven', a poetic name for manna. KJV 'corn' means grain. Radak says manna was eaten in place of grain, and better; Metzudat David calls it a doubling of 'manna'.
Hiphil of 'to rain': he made it rain. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David both read the narrative form as a pluperfect, 'he had already rained'.

verses.translation_literal: Bread of [the] mighty ones a man ate; provisions he sent to them to satiety.
verses.translation_dramatic: Mortals ate the bread of the mighty ones. Out of the sky it came, bread fit for the strong, and the LORD kept sending provisions until no one was hungry any more.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse opens with a startling phrase: 'bread of the mighty ones.' The word אַבִּירִים is the plural of a word for the strong (also used of bulls and warriors elsewhere), and here it names whoever stands above ordinary men. The Targum, Rashi and Radak all take it as beings of the heavens; Radak reads it as the skies themselves. The KJV's 'angels' food' follows that tradition, but the Hebrew never says 'angels', so a director should keep the word large and a little strange. The key is the contrast: 'a man' (אִישׁ, an ordinary person made of earth, as Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David note) ate what the heavens eat. This looks back to the manna, and the phrase invites the audience to be amazed.

The second half says he 'sent provisions.' צֵידָה comes from the root for hunting, and means food for the road, travel rations. The KJV's 'meat' is misleading, since in 1611 'meat' meant any food and it will sound like flesh to a modern ear. This matters because the next verses are about real meat. The verb 'sent' is the same one the psalm will keep using for God's deliveries. 'To satiety' (לָשֹׂבַע) is a sound that will return in v. 29.

philological_notes.note: 'Mighty ones'. The plural of 'abbir, 'strong, mighty'. The traditions in the packet take it as beings of the heavens (Targum, Rashi, Radak, Metzudat David); Rashi's second reading connects it with אֵיבָרִים, limbs. The word itself does not say 'angels'.
'Provisions', food taken on a journey; related to the root for hunting. Ibn Ezra explains it by the people's constant travelling.

verses.translation_literal: He set out an east wind in the heavens, and he led forth by his strength a south wind.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then he broke camp in the heavens and sent the east wind out, and by his strength he drove the south wind after it, like a shepherd leading a flock across the sky.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb יַסַּע is the word for striking the tents and setting out on the march. All through the wilderness story it describes Israel's own journeys. Here God makes the wind journey, and the second verb, וַיְנַהֵג, is 'drove, led', as a herdsman drives animals. The wind is a creature on the move, marching at his orders. The KJV's 'caused to blow' and 'brought in' flatten both of these into weather reports.

The winds themselves are precise. קָדִים is the east wind, the hot desert wind that scorches in the Bible. תֵּימָן is literally 'right-hand side', the south, because the ancient speaker faces the sunrise (Ibn Ezra derives it from ימין). Together they point to a south-east wind. Radak and Metzudat David say the wind came from that corner, and Malbim argues that it is a miracle precisely because such a wind would blow the quail away from Israel. Rashi quotes Numbers 11:31 for the event. Play 'by his strength' (בְּעֻזּוֹ) with weight: the wind obeys.

philological_notes.note: From נסע, 'pull up (tent pegs), set out'; the standard verb for the stages of the wilderness march. The wind is made to travel like a camp.
'South', literally the right-hand side, since the speaker faces east. Ibn Ezra derives it from ימין and says it is the south-east wind.

verses.translation_literal: And he rained upon them flesh like the dust, and like [the] sand of [the] seas, bird[s] of wing.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the sky rained down on them. Flesh fell thick as dust, birds fell numberless as the sand along the shores of the seas, every one of them winged, and every one of them falling.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image is 'it rained flesh.' וַיַּמְטֵר is the verb for rain, and the poet uses it on purpose: a downpour, not a handful. שְׁאֵר is the common word for flesh, meat, and also for one's close kin. The KJV's 'flesh' is accurate here, though a modern reader hears it as raw anatomy; the Hebrew intends food, and the shock is the quantity. Two comparisons pile up: 'like dust' and 'like the sand of the seas', the standard biblical measures of what cannot be counted. Radak and Meiri both stress that the birds came 'in great number like rain'. Malbim adds that they were dropped, not flying off, 'like dust falling down'.

The last words, עוֹף כָּנָף, are literally 'bird of wing.' It is an odd phrase because every bird has wings. The KJV's 'feathered fowls' tries to explain it, but the Hebrew is simply emphatic and a little poetic: winged things, as though to say they could have flown away and did not. Hold the beat before 'bird of wing' and let the last syllable fall.

philological_notes.note: 'Flesh, meat'; Rashi glosses it בָּשָׂר. The same word means 'close relative' elsewhere, but here it is food.
Literally 'bird of wing', a pleonastic phrase for winged birds; Metzudat David glosses it 'a bird that has a wing'.

verses.translation_literal: And he made [it] fall in [the] midst of his camp, round about, to his dwellings.
verses.translation_dramatic: He let them drop into the very middle of the camp, all around, up to the doors of the tents, so that no one needed to go out and hunt for what had come down for them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb וַיַּפֵּל is causative: 'he made it fall.' The text names no object, and the audience supplies the flesh and the birds of the verse before. Hebrew gives two locations: 'in the midst of his camp', and 'round about, to his dwellings' (the word for dwellings, מִשְׁכָּנוֹת, is the plural of the word used for the tabernacle). The KJV and ASV smooth over a small oddity: the Hebrew says 'his camp' and 'his dwellings', in the singular, while they translate 'their'. YLT keeps the singular and reads it as God's camp. The sense is Israel's camp, as the next verse shows, but the singular 'his' can make the listener wonder for a moment whose camp it is.

The practical point is made by Metzudat David: they did not have to chase after the birds. Malbim adds that birds normally keep away from people, yet these fell close, and not on the roofs of the tents. The laying out of the dead birds around the tents is the picture to play: abundance as a ring around the sleepers.

philological_notes.note: 'His dwellings', from מִשְׁכָּן, the word also used for the tabernacle. Ibn Ezra says it means the tents, like 'camp'.

verses.translation_literal: And they ate, and they were sated exceedingly, and their craving he brings to them.
verses.translation_dramatic: So they ate. They ate and ate until they were glutted, because what they craved, he had brought to them.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the long build-up the action is only two short words: 'and they ate, and they were sated.' The sounds repeat the לָשֹׂבַע of v. 25, and the satiety there is now fulfilled, with the weight on מְאֹד, 'exceedingly.' The KJV 'well filled' is mild; Radak says 'more than enough.' There is no gloating in the text, but there is an edge.

The second half turns it. תַּאֲוָה is 'craving, lust', a strong appetite, and the root belongs to the wilderness place named for this very episode, the Graves of Craving (Num 11:34). The KJV 'he gave them their own desire' is a clean paraphrase and makes God sound indulgent. The Hebrew verb is an imperfect, יָבִא, 'he brings', so the sense is of a repeated giving: whatever they craved, he kept bringing. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'he used to bring'. Malbim's long note says that this is meant to show the real sin was rebellion, not appetite. The audience should hear satisfaction and warning in the same breath.

philological_notes.note: 'Craving, desire'; strong appetite, usually in a negative sense in the wilderness narratives. It sets up the next verse.
Imperfect 'he brings', habitual: whatever they craved he kept bringing. Ibn Ezra explains the tense as 'he used to bring'.

verses.translation_literal: They were not estranged from their craving; still their food [was] in their mouths.
verses.translation_dramatic: They had not yet turned away from their craving. The food was still in their mouths.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a verse built to be held and then broken off. 'They were not estranged from their craving' uses the verb זוּר, 'to turn aside, become a stranger' (it gives the word for 'stranger' זָר). Their craving was still their close companion and had not become foreign to them. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read it as 'they had not yet become disgusted', and Ibn Ezra's association with Numbers 11:20, the meat that would 'come out of your nostrils' and become זָרָא, 'loathsome', is the sound play behind it. The KJV 'lust' is stronger than the Hebrew requires, but 'craving' keeps the sense.

The second half is a picture a director can play literally: 'their food in their mouths.' Radak and Rashi connect this to Numbers 11:33, 'the meat was still between their teeth, before it was chewed'. The sentence is left open, with no finite verb in the second half. In the KJV the clause runs on into v. 31 ('But while their meat was yet in their mouths, the wrath of God...'), and that is correct: the text stops mid-bite and the audience waits for the blow.

philological_notes.note: 'They had turned aside / become estranged'; from the root of זָר 'stranger'. Rashi: they had not become strangers to their craving, for they had got all of it. Ibn Ezra links it to loathing.
'Their food'; the noun 'okhel, with the possessive suffix, in its mouth.

verses.translation_literal: And [the] anger of God went up against them, and he killed among their fat ones, and [the] young men of Israel he made bow down.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the anger of God rose up against them like smoke. It struck down the strongest among them, and it brought down the young men of Israel, the best of them, to their knees and onto the ground.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew says אַף, which is both 'anger' and 'nose': the nose flares and flames when someone burns with fury. 'The nose of God went up' is the same picture as the idiom 'his nose burned'. Radak compares 'smoke went up in his nostril' (Ps 18:9). The KJV 'wrath of God came upon them' replaces a bodily image with an abstraction. The verb 'went up' (עָלָה) is also the verb for rising smoke or a rising flame, so the anger rises like heat.

Then the victims. בְּמִשְׁמַנֵּיהֶם is literally 'among their fat ones', from the word for oil and fat. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read it as an adjective, 'the sturdy, the vigorous, the important'. The KJV 'fattest' keeps the fat. Either way the point is that the victims are the healthy and the privileged. Then בַּחוּרֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל: 'young men', which the KJV renders 'chosen men' (from the root בחר, to choose; Rashi and Metzudat David take it that way). The final verb הִכְרִיעַ is 'made kneel, bow down', and the KJV 'smote down' loses the posture: they were brought to their knees. A director should show the strongest going first.

philological_notes.note: Both 'anger' and 'nose'. The idiom of anger rising in the nose; Ibn Ezra and Radak compare other verses that use 'went up' of anger or smoke.
'Among their fat ones'; from שמן 'oil, fat'. Radak and Meiri take it as an adjective meaning 'the healthy and strong among them'; Ibn Ezra, 'the great and wealthy'.
'He made bow down, kneel'; Metzudat Zion glosses it as falling on the knees.

verses.translation_literal: In all this they sinned again, and they did not believe in his wonders.
verses.translation_dramatic: And still, after all of this, they sinned again. They would not trust him, not for all his wonders.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is short and heavy, a sigh. 'In all this' (בְּכָל זֹאת) means 'in spite of everything': the manna, the quail and the deaths. The KJV 'for all this' is acceptable, but a modern ear takes 'for' as 'because'. Then עוֹד, 'again, still'. The Hebrew is not a new sin but the old one continuing.

The second half is where the KJV and its siblings get the grammar wrong. They write 'believed not for his wondrous works', as if the wonders were the reason for belief or unbelief. The Hebrew has הֶאֱמִינוּ בְּ, 'believed in', and the object is the wonders themselves: they did not put their trust in them. The verb הֶאֱמִין is the one that gives 'amen', 'firm, to be relied on'; faith here is reliance, not an opinion. The commentators in the packet point to the spies and the refusal to enter the land (Radak, Meiri, Malbim) as the sin in view, and the next verse is the sentence. Play it flat and tired, not angry.

philological_notes.note: 'They believed, trusted'; the hiphil of אמן, 'be firm, reliable', which also gives 'amen'. With ב it means to put trust in something.
'In his wonders'; the nifal participle of פלא, things too extraordinary to explain. The KJV 'for his wondrous works' mistakes the ב.

verses.translation_literal: And he finished in [the] breath their days, and their years in [the] sudden terror.
verses.translation_dramatic: So he spent their days like a breath, a puff of vapor, and their years went in panic.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verbs of finishing are about to eat the calendar. וַיְכַל is 'he finished, brought to an end' (the root of 'complete'), and the object is the people's whole time: days and years. The KJV 'consume in vanity' hides the image. הֶבֶל is 'breath, vapor', the very word of Ecclesiastes ('vapor of vapors'); a life that is a puff of steam. The KJV and ASV renderings, 'vanity', 'trouble', 'terror', are abstractions, and BBE's 'like a breath' is closest to the image.

The second noun is בֶּהָלָה, 'sudden terror, panic', and the poet plays with the letters: הֶבֶל and בֶּהָלָה contain the same three consonants, ה ב ל, in a different order (h-b-l, b-h-l), so the verse sounds like breath turned to panic. Radak notes the definite article ('in the terror'), referring to the known panic, and Meiri says 'the known plague'. The traditional commentators (Radak, Malbim) tie this to the forty years in the wilderness, so the phrase covers a generation: a long march in which each year was a funeral. It is the sentence the audience has been waiting for.

philological_notes.note: 'Breath, vapor', then 'futility'. It is the word that gives Ecclesiastes its refrain, and its sound is echoed by בֶּהָלָה.
'In the sudden terror, panic'. Radak points out that the definite article refers to a known event; Meiri reads it as the plague.

verses.translation_literal: If he killed them, then they sought him, and they returned, and they sought God earnestly.
verses.translation_dramatic: Whenever he struck them down, they came looking for him. They turned around, they rose early, they sought God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The conditional אִם with a past verb is best heard as 'whenever': it is a pattern, not a single event. Radak and Meiri say so, and the KJV, ASV and Webster agree with 'when he slew them'. Notice what the verse is saying: repentance followed death every time.

Three verbs of return pile up: 'they sought' (דָּרַשׁ, to inquire of, consult), 'they returned' (שׁוּב, the basic verb of turning back and repentance), and 'they sought earnestly' (שָׁחַר). שָׁחַר is related to שַׁחַר, 'dawn', so it means to look for someone at first light, as the KJV's 'enquired early' tries to keep. Ibn Ezra says it is the morning prayer, said before a man begins his own business. It is intense and eager, and an audience should hear how convincing it is.

The last word, אֵל, is a name of God without a definite article, and the verse uses 'God' (אֵל) after earlier 'him'. Rashi, reading ahead, says this repentance was not sincere, but the verse does not yet say so; let it sound sincere so that v. 36 can reverse it.

philological_notes.note: 'They sought earnestly'; related to שַׁחַר 'dawn', so 'seek at daybreak'. Ibn Ezra connects it to morning prayer; Metzudat Zion to the sense of seeking, as in שוֹחֵר טוֹב.
'If' with a past verb; Radak and Meiri read it as 'when, whenever', which gives a repeated pattern.

verses.translation_literal: And they remembered that God [was] their rock, and God Most High their redeemer.
verses.translation_dramatic: And they remembered. God was their Rock, they said, and God Most High was the one who had bought them back.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two titles are laid side by side, each a pillar. צוּר, 'rock', is the image of a cliff or mountain refuge, a place where a hunted man can stand; the KJV leaves it as 'rock', which is right. גֹּאֵל is a legal word, not just a religious one. A גֹּאֵל is the family's 'redeemer' who buys back property sold in debt, rescues a relative from slavery or takes up a dead kinsman's cause. 'Redeemer' in the KJV is correct, but it is such a church word now that the legal force is lost: a relative who pays the price. The title אֵל עֶלְיוֹן, 'God Most High', is an old and exalted title (used for the God of Abraham in Genesis 14), and Ibn Ezra says it points to the one who can do anything he wants on the earth.

The verb is 'they remembered', but in Hebrew זָכַר means to bring something to mind and act on it. Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David and Malbim all say it was in the mouth only; the heart was not in it. The text leaves the hint to the next verse. Play it as a recital, a creed repeated by people who have been frightened.

philological_notes.note: 'Their rock', an image of refuge and strength. Ibn Ezra glosses it 'their strength'.
'Their redeemer', the family redeemer of the law who buys back, frees or avenges a relative.
'God Most High'. Ibn Ezra explains that the one who redeemed them is Most High, able to do whatever he wills on earth.

verses.translation_literal: And they coaxed him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: But it was all in the mouth. They coaxed him with their lips, and their tongues lied to him.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse takes the previous one apart. 'Remembered' was words only. The verb וַיְפַתּוּהוּ is from פָּתָה, 'to entice, persuade, dupe': it is what a seducer does, and what Proverbs says a fool is, פֶּתִי, easily led. The KJV's 'flatter' is too soft, because flattery is a social nicety, and the Hebrew is closer to 'tried to get around him'. YLT's 'deceive' is nearer. The grammar is sharp: the people are the subject and God is the object, so the creature is trying to charm the Creator.

The body does the work: 'with their mouth', 'with their tongue.' Both are instruments of speech and the two organs of the lie, set against the heart, which the next verse will mention. The second verb, יְכַזְּבוּ, 'they lied', is an intensive form, so the lies are repeated, not a slip. The KJV makes the sentence sound like a polite complaint ('Nevertheless'); the Hebrew simply starts with 'and'. Radak and Meiri point out the irony: God cannot be coaxed, since he knows the heart; Metzudat David says they were not wholehearted. A director should let the voice drop at the end of the verse, with a hush, since the audience has just been taken in as well.

philological_notes.note: 'And they coaxed / deceived him'; piel of פתה, 'entice, persuade, dupe'. Radak and Meiri stress that God cannot actually be fooled, and that the verse describes what they thought they were doing.
'They lied'; piel imperfect, repeated lying. Rashi says they lied with their tongue what they did not say in truth.

verses.translation_literal: And their heart [was] not steadfast with him, and they were not faithful in his covenant.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the heart in them was never fixed to him. It shifted like sand under a standing man, and the covenant they had sworn they did not hold.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hinge of the psalm: the lips of the previous verses said the right things, and now the narrator names the gap. 'Heart' in Hebrew is the seat of will and decision more than of feeling, so 'their heart was not steadfast' is a charge of disloyalty, not of sadness. The verb נָכוֹן is the root of 'firm, set in place', and נֶאֶמְנוּ is the root of 'amen': the two words together say 'not fixed, not amen-ed'. 'In his covenant' is the language of a treaty: the vassal's faithfulness is what is at stake. The KJV 'right with him' and 'stedfast' are fair, but 'right' loses the sense of physical firmness that the root carries, and the ASV 'faithful' catches the second verb better than the KJV.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of 'to be firm, set up'. Used of a heart it means fixed in loyalty; the same word describes a house standing on its foundations. The psalm's verdict is about stability, not sincerity of feeling.
Niphal of the root behind 'amen' and 'emunah': to prove reliable. Paired with נָכוֹן it makes a wordplay on firmness and trustworthiness.

verses.translation_literal: And he [is] compassionate: he covers iniquity and does not destroy, and he multiplies to turn back his anger, and does not rouse all his rage.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet he. He, who is full of mercy, covers the guilt and does not strike them down. Again and again he turns his anger aside, and never once does he rouse the whole of his fury.
verses.directors_commentary: The sentence turns on the word 'and he': a short pronoun placed first, as an emphatic contrast to the faithless 'they' of verse 37. The verbs are imperfects and mean a habit, not a single event: this is what he regularly does. 'Covers' is the literal sense of כִּפֶּר, the verb of atonement, which in the ritual world means to wipe or cover over the offence, not merely to forgive it. 'Multiplies to turn back' is an idiom for 'does so many times', and the KJV 'many a time turned he his anger away' catches it, though it reads smoothly where the Hebrew is odd. The two words for anger are not the same: אַף is the nose that snorts, the visible flare, and חֵמָה is the heat in the chest; Malbim distinguishes the outer, punishing anger from the inner, stored one. The KJV 'forgave' and 'destroyed them not' put the verbs in the past, where the Hebrew gives a pattern that holds true still.

philological_notes.note: Piel of 'to cover'. The ritual verb of atonement; here God is the subject, who covers over the guilt himself. Ibn Ezra reads the imperfect as describing a standing state.
'Nose', then 'anger': Hebrew imagines the flare of the nostrils. Contrasted with חֲמָתוֹ 'his heat', the inner rage. Malbim distinguishes them as outward and inward anger.
'He multiplied to turn back': an idiom for repeated action ('many times'), as Rashi glosses 'many times'.

verses.translation_literal: And he remembered that they [are] flesh, a wind going and not returning.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he remembered what they were: flesh, no more. A breath that goes out and does not come back.
verses.directors_commentary: God 'remembers', a verb that in Hebrew means to act on what one knows, and what he remembers is the frailty of his people. 'Flesh' (בָּשָׂר) is the creaturely side of a human being, weak and short-lived, not a moral judgment; the KJV 'but flesh' adds a 'but' that the Hebrew does not have, though it fits the tone. 'Wind' and 'breath' are one word, רוּחַ: the psalmist sees a life as air passing through, which makes God's patience a response to how little time they have. The last clause 'and does not return' refers to ordinary death, as Radak says, not a denial of resurrection; he notes that God can still return the breath to the flesh. KJV 'passeth away' smooths the participle הוֹלֵךְ, 'going', which in Hebrew is still moving.

philological_notes.note: Wind, breath or spirit. Here it is both: a wind that blows and does not come back, and the breath of life that leaves the body. Radak reads 'does not return' as the natural order of death, not a denial of resurrection.
Flesh: the body as the frail, mortal side of the person. Radak and Metzudat David connect it to appetite and the tendency to sin; the plain sense is mortality.

verses.translation_literal: How often they rebelled against him in the wilderness, they grieved him in the desolation.
verses.translation_dramatic: How often! In the wilderness they defied him, and in the empty waste they gave him grief.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker breaks off into an exclamation, and the voice should show it. The two lines say the same thing in parallel: 'wilderness' (מִדְבָּר) and 'desolation' (יְשִׁימוֹן) are a pair of synonyms for the same open desert, and the two verbs 'rebel' and 'grieve' are a pair as well; Radak and Meiri both note the doubling. The second verb, עָצַב, is the root of 'pain, sorrow': God is hurt, not only angered, and that is unusual language for a deity in the ancient Near East, where gods are offended but rarely grieved. The KJV 'provoke' is weaker than 'rebel', which is the force of מָרָה: to rebel against a lawful ruler. The KJV 'desert' for יְשִׁימוֹן hides the sense of 'waste' or 'emptiness'.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'to be rebellious'. A political word: defying an authority, so 'rebel' is closer than the KJV's 'provoke'. Radak glosses it as making him angry by changing his commands.
Hiphil of 'to hurt, grieve'; the noun עֶצֶב is pain or sorrow. Ibn Ezra takes it as a figure drawn from עִצָּבוֹן.

verses.translation_literal: And they turned back and tested God, and the Holy One of Israel they set a mark on.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then they turned again, and they put God to the proof. They drew a line around the Holy One of Israel and dared him to cross it.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Turned back' (וַיָּשׁוּבוּ) is the same root שׁוּב as the 'return' of verse 39, but with the opposite moral direction: the wind does not come back, and the people do, only to fall again. 'Tested' (נִסָּה) is the word used for the incident at Massah, 'Is the LORD among us or not?' (Exod 17:7), which Rashi cites on this verse. The last verb, הִתְווּ, comes from תָּוָה, 'to make a mark', related to the letter תָּו (tav) that was a cross-shaped sign. Radak and Malbim read it as 'they set a limit around him', treating God as one whose power has an edge; Rashi reads it as 'they demanded a sign'. KJV 'limited' follows the first. ASV 'provoked' and BBE 'gave pain' go another way. The title 'Holy One of Israel' is placed at the end, by contrast: the people draw a boundary around the one who is set apart.

philological_notes.note: From תָּוָה, 'to mark'; the noun תָּו is a mark or sign (Ezek 9:4). Read either as 'they marked out a limit for him' (Radak, Meiri, Malbim) or 'they demanded a sign' (Rashi). A rare form, and uncertain.
To test, put to the proof. Radak ties it to Massah and Meribah and to other trials not told in the Torah.

verses.translation_literal: They did not remember his hand, [the] day [when] he ransomed them from [the] adversary.
verses.translation_dramatic: They did not remember his hand, nor the day he bought them back from the grip of the enemy.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Hand' is power, and 'the day' is a single, datable event: the Exodus, the moment of rescue. The verb פָּדָה is a market word, 'to ransom, to buy back', used of redeeming a slave or a firstborn; this places the Exodus in the vocabulary of a purchase, with God as the one who pays. The KJV 'delivered' is a fair rendering of the outcome but loses the commercial image, which ASV's 'redeemed' keeps. 'Adversary' is צַר, from the root 'to be tight', so 'the one who squeezes'; there is a wordplay with Egypt, מִצְרַיִם, in the next verse. Malbim notes that the forgetting began on the very day of the rescue, at the sea.

philological_notes.note: To ransom or redeem: a payment to free a person from bondage. The Exodus is cast as a buy-back.
'Adversary', from the root 'to be narrow, to bind'. Sounds like מִצְרַיִם (Egypt) in the next verse, which may be intended.

verses.translation_literal: How he set in Egypt his signs, and his wonders in the field of Zoan.
verses.translation_dramatic: They forgot how he had set his signs down in Egypt, planted his wonders in the open country of Zoan, where no one could miss them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse looks back from the forgetting of v.42 to the thing forgotten, and it opens a catalogue of plagues (vv.44–51). Play it as an accusation by recital: the speaker does not argue, he lists, and the listing is the argument. Israel's memory is the subject of the psalm, and each remembered act is a debt.

The verb שָׂם, 'set', is deliberate: God does not merely 'work' signs, he places them like markers on the ground. KJV 'wrought' and BBE 'done' flatten that image; YLT and ASV 'set' are closer. The line is a poetic parallel. 'Signs' (אוֹתוֹת) and 'wonders' (מוֹפְתִים) are the standard Exodus pair, and 'in Egypt' and 'in the field of Zoan' answer one another. Radak says the verse doubles the idea in different words, as is the custom. Meiri reads 'field of Zoan' as 'land of Zoan', like 'field of Aram', so that both halves name the same country. Ibn Ezra notes the prophet speaks of these signs as the great wonders they were. Malbim instead assigns signs to Egypt as a teaching and wonders to Zoan as a blow to the land; that is a later schematic reading and not required by the Hebrew.

The place matters for the first audience. Zoan is Djanet (Greek Tanis), a major Delta city and a royal seat in the Ramesside and later periods. As background, it lay in the northeastern Delta, in the region of Goshen, near where Israel lived. 'Field' (שָׂדֶה) here means the territory around a city, as in 'the field of Aram', and does not mean farmland. The psalmist puts the plagues at the doorstep of Pharaoh's court, and Num 13:22 supplies the Israelite sense of Zoan as an old and proud city. The point is polemical: the gods of Egypt are shown up in their own capital. KJV's 'field of Zoan' is literal and correct, but modern readers hear a meadow where the Hebrew hears a province.

philological_notes.note: 'His signs': a sign is something that points beyond itself and shows who acts. Paired with מוֹפְתָיו 'his wonders' as the stock Exodus pair.
'In the field of Zoan': שָׂדֶה means open country around a place. Zoan is Djanet (Greek Tanis) in the northeastern Delta. Meiri takes 'field of Zoan' as 'land of Zoan', like 'field of Aram'.

verses.translation_literal: And he turned to blood their Nile-channels, and their streams, they could not drink.
verses.translation_dramatic: He turned their rivers to blood, and the streams that fed them ran red, and no one could drink.
verses.directors_commentary: The first plague. The word יְאֹר is an Egyptian loanword, itr, meaning the Nile and the canals cut from it; Metzudat Zion calls them man-made pools, and the word is plural, so the picture is the whole irrigation network of the Delta, on which every field and household depended. The KJV 'rivers' and 'floods' both soften the picture: נֹזְלִים are 'flowing things', water that runs by itself, so the verse covers the channels and the natural runoff. The last clause uses בַּל, a poetic 'not', in an imperfect: 'they could not drink' or 'would not'. In a land with almost no rain, undrinkable water is a death sentence, and the Egyptians worshipped the Nile as a source of life; a plague that turns it to blood is a blow aimed at that religion.

philological_notes.note: From Egyptian itrw, 'river', the Nile; in the plural it means the Nile's channels and canals. Metzudat Zion takes them as man-made pools.
Poetic negative with a long imperfect form ending in -ūn; 'they could not drink'.

verses.translation_literal: He sent among them a swarm, and it ate them, and frog, and it ruined them.
verses.translation_dramatic: He sent a swarm among them, and it devoured them. He sent the frogs, and they laid waste to them.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm gives the plagues in its own order, not Exodus's; it is a poem, not a ledger, as Radak and Meiri both remark. The word עָרֹב is only 'a mixture, a swarm'; the Hebrew does not say what kind. Metzudat Zion reads it as a mixture of beasts, the Targum as wild animals, and the KJV 'divers sorts of flies' follows the Greek tradition, though the Hebrew does not say 'flies'. A singular 'frog' (צְפַרְדֵּעַ) is used for a whole swarm, as Radak says, a collective like 'locust'. The verb 'ate' with a swarm and 'ruined' with a frog is a clear exaggeration, since a frog does not eat a man; the verb שָׁחַת is 'to corrupt', so the frogs fouled the land. In Egypt the frog was a sacred animal, linked with the goddess Heqet, so the plague turns a symbol of fertility into a nuisance.

philological_notes.note: 'Mixture', 'swarm'. The Hebrew does not name the creature. Metzudat Zion: a mixture of kinds of animals. The Targum has wild beasts; the KJV 'flies' is a tradition, not the Hebrew.
'Frog', in the singular as a collective; Radak: a general name for frogs.

verses.translation_literal: And he gave to the hasil their produce, and their toil to the locust.
verses.translation_dramatic: He gave their harvest to the devouring locust, and the fruit of all their labour to the swarm.
verses.directors_commentary: Two words for locust, חָסִיל and אַרְבֶּה, set in parallel: Meiri says they are one thing, Metzudat Zion that the first is a kind of locust. The KJV renders the first 'caterpiller', which is a guess; the word is a locust in a stage or kind we cannot fix. The pairing of 'produce' (יְבוּל) and 'toil' (יְגִיעַ) is the important one: the second word means 'what one's work has won', so the crop is not only food but the sweat of a year. Metzudat David notes that the doubling is the poet's. In an agrarian world a locust swarm means a year of famine, and it is the loss of effort, not just grain, that the psalm lingers on. The verb 'gave' (נָתַן) makes the locust a recipient, as if the crop were a gift passed to another owner.

philological_notes.note: A kind of locust, from the root 'to consume'. The KJV 'caterpiller' is a guess. Meiri: the same as אַרְבֶּה; Metzudat Zion: a type of locust.
'The product of toil', not only labour: what weary work has won. Metzudat David: the crop that comes through labour.

token_glosses.gloss: and the fruit of their toil

verses.translation_literal: He killed with the hail their vine, and their sycamore-figs with chanamal.
verses.translation_dramatic: He struck down their vines with hail, and their sycamores with the killing frost.
verses.directors_commentary: Verbs of killing are used of plants: הָרַג, 'to slay', is the word for murder, and the poem lets the vineyards die like men. Radak and Meiri say the word is borrowed, a figure like 'you shall ruin every good field with stones' (2 Kgs 3:19). The sycamore fig (שִׁקְמָה) was the common timber tree of Egypt and its fruit the food of the poor, so the blow falls on both luxury, the vine, and daily bread. The word חֲנָמַל appears only here, and nobody knows it: Rashi takes it as a locust, Ibn Ezra as large stones, Radak and Meiri, with Saadia, as hard ice or frost. KJV 'frost' follows the third, and I keep it; STEPBible's 'flood' has no support in the commentators here. The sound is odd and heavy, so it should be spoken slowly.

philological_notes.note: A word found only here; its meaning is disputed: a locust (Rashi), a large stone or hailstone (Ibn Ezra), hard frost or ice (Radak, Meiri, citing Saadia). I take 'frost'.
Sycamore-fig, a large tree producing a small, cheap fig; common in Egypt and the lowlands of Israel. Radak: a wild kind of fig.

verses.translation_literal: And he shut up to the hail their cattle, and their livestock to the reshaphim.
verses.translation_dramatic: He gave their cattle over to the hail, and their herds to the bolts of fire.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb הִסְגִּיר is 'to hand over, to deliver up', as one hands a prisoner to his captors: the animals are given over, not merely hit. Meiri cites the law that one must not hand over a runaway slave to his master (Deut 23:16) for the same verb. The last word, רְשָׁפִים, is 'flames' or 'sparks': Rashi's plain reading and Radak both link it to the fire that ran among the hail in Exod 9:24. The KJV's 'hot thunderbolts' catches the sense. The word is also the name of Resheph, the West Semitic god of plague and fire, and the audience may have heard that echo as well: the plural here makes the god's name into a common noun for his weapons. That is my own reading and is not in the commentaries. The listener should feel the escalation: first crops, now animals, and the pace of the verse speeds up.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'to shut': 'to hand over', as in Deut 23:16. Meiri and Metzudat Zion take it as 'delivering up'.
'Flames, bolts of fire'; compare Exod 9:24, the fire flashing in the hail. Rashi also records a midrash reading it as 'birds'. The word is also the name of the Canaanite god of plague, Resheph.

verses.translation_literal: He sends on them the burning of his nose, fury and indignation and trouble, a sending of messengers of evils.
verses.translation_dramatic: He loosed upon them the blaze of his anger: fury, and rage, and distress, a whole company of ill-boding messengers sent out at his word.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb is a present-tense-looking imperfect, ‘he would send’, and the psalmist piles up four near-synonyms for anger before the climax, so the actor should let the voice climb through them rather than treat them as a list. The first is the ancient idiom חֲרוֹן אַף, ‘the burning of the nose’: in Hebrew a man in rage literally flares his nostrils, and the KJV’s ‘fierceness of his anger’ flattens the body out of it.

The last phrase, מִשְׁלַחַת מַלְאֲכֵי רָעִים, is a trap. The KJV makes the plagues ‘evil angels’, which sounds like demons. Radak and Meiri read it as ‘evil [i.e. destructive] messengers’, and say the plagues themselves were the envoys, sent at God’s will; Ibn Ezra compares Psalm 104:4, ‘who makes the winds his messengers, flaming fire his servants’. The word מַלְאָךְ is just ‘one who is sent’, and the root שָׁלַח, ‘send’, frames the line twice (‘he sends’ … ‘a sending’). The verse is also a summary: Meiri reads the five terms as covering the five plagues the psalm has not named.

philological_notes.note: ‘The burning of his nose’: anger as heat in the nostrils, a stock idiom for divine wrath. The raw physical image is kept in the literal layer.
Literally ‘messengers of evils’. Radak and Meiri take it as an unbound ‘evil messengers’, the plagues as God’s envoys; Ibn Ezra offers the fire-and-wind parallel of Ps 104:4.

verses.translation_literal: He levels a path for his nose; he did not hold back their soul from death, and their life he handed over to the pestilence.
verses.translation_dramatic: He smoothed a road for his anger and let it run. Their breath he did not hold back from death; their very lives he gave up to the plague.
verses.directors_commentary:
‘He weighs out a path for his anger’: the verb פָּלַס is the one used for leveling a road or for the balance-beam, so the picture is a god who surveys the ground and clears it for his wrath. The KJV’s ‘he made a way’ is correct but loses the surveyor’s care; Metzudat Zion ties it to Proverbs 4:26, ‘level the track of your feet’, and to the beam of the scales. Malbim reads the verb as weighing, a controlled, measured anger.

The second half is hard because וְחַיָּתָם can mean ‘their life’ (Ibn Ezra, Radak: the same as נַפְשָׁם) or ‘their animals’ (Metzudat Zion; one reading Radak reports), which suits the cattle plague of Exodus 9. Rashi has ‘their bodies’. The KJV ‘spared not’ turns לֹא חָשַׂךְ, ‘did not hold back’, into a gentler word. The verb הִסְגִּיר is ‘shut up, hand over’, the language of delivering a prisoner or surrendering a city.

philological_notes.note: To level, weigh, make a path smooth; also the root of פֶּלֶס, ‘balance’. Radak: ‘he made straight a way for his anger’; Metzudat Zion links it to Prov 4:26.
‘Their life’ (Ibn Ezra, Radak) or ‘their cattle’ (Metzudat Zion). Rashi: ‘their bodies’.
To shut up, deliver over; used of handing a captive or a city to an enemy.

verses.translation_literal: And he struck every firstborn in Egypt, the first of vigor in the tents of Ham.
