verses.translation_dramatic: And then he struck down the firstborn, every one, in Egypt: the first fruit of their strength, in the tents of Ham.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the last and greatest of the plagues, and the verse is built to ring: ‘struck’, ‘every firstborn’, then the doubling ‘first … of vigor’. The word אוֹנִים is not an abstract ‘strength’. It is the vigor of a father’s manhood, the same as the firstborn Reuben in Genesis 49:3, ‘my might and the first of my vigor’. The firstborn is the first proof of a man’s potency, and in the world of the psalm the firstborn carries the family name and estate, so the blow lands on the household’s future. The KJV’s ‘chief of their strength’ keeps the sense but softens the sexual edge.

‘Tents of Ham’ is a deliberate archaic pairing: Egypt is descended from Ham (Genesis 10:6), and Ibn Ezra says naming the ancestor is a way of shaming them, Radak simply that Ham is the father of Egypt. Calling a settled, pyramid-building nation by its ancestor’s tents is a sneer. The KJV ‘tabernacles’ would suggest a sanctuary, where the Hebrew means plain tents.

philological_notes.note: ‘First of vigor’: the firstborn as the first fruit of a father’s manhood, as in Gen 49:3 (Metzudat David) and Hos 12:9 (Metzudat Zion).
‘Tents of Ham’: Egypt named by its ancestor. Ibn Ezra says this is shaming; Radak, only that Ham is the father of Egypt.

verses.translation_literal: And he made his people set out like the flock, and led them like the herd in the wilderness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then he pulled up the stakes of his own people, like a shepherd breaking camp, and drove them gently on through the wilderness, a herd at his heels.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood changes. After three verses of wrath the psalm turns to the shepherd. Both verbs are shepherd’s verbs: נָסַע is to pull up the tent pegs and set out, and נָהַג is to drive or lead livestock. The two similes, ‘like the flock’ and ‘like the herd’, are parallel, and each uses the definite article in Hebrew (‘the flock’), as of a flock the listener knows. The KJV reverses the order of the clauses (‘made … go forth like sheep, and guided … like a flock’), which hides the symmetry.

Ibn Ezra stresses that ‘like sheep’ means slowly, at the pace of the weakest animal; Metzudat David and Malbim that the shepherd finds grazing in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing. Everything in the image is the opposite of the Egypt of the previous verse: a people led, not driven by taskmasters.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of נסע: to pull up the tent pegs and set out; here causative, ‘he made them break camp’.
To drive or lead, used of flocks and of chariots; the shepherd’s verb.

verses.translation_literal: And he guided them to security, and they did not fear; and their enemies the sea covered.
verses.translation_dramatic: He led them to safety and they were not afraid. And their enemies? The sea closed over them.
verses.directors_commentary:
‘To security’ (לָבֶטַח) is the word of a flock lying down unthreatened; the shepherd image from the last verse carries on. The statement ‘they did not fear’ is a poetic compression: Exodus 14:10 says they feared greatly. Radak and Meiri solve it as a matter of the moment: Moses told them at once ‘Fear not’, and they saw the Egyptians dead; Malbim says that, unlike sheep in the wilderness with their fear of wild beasts, they were not afraid because the sea took their enemies. Read it as a moment of rest after the shock, not as a claim about the whole journey.

The Hebrew word order puts the enemies first (‘and their enemies — the sea covered’), a sudden turn. The KJV’s ‘overwhelmed’ is the translator’s own, where the verb is כָּסָה, ‘covered’, the same as Exodus 15:5, ‘the depths covered them’. Ibn Ezra’s other reading, that the safe path was on dry ground through the sea, rests on the sense of ‘guided to security’ as the crossing itself.

philological_notes.note: ‘To security, in confidence’: the safety of a flock or a settled people.
‘Covered’; the KJV ‘overwhelmed’ is an interpretation. The word echoes Ex 15:5.

verses.translation_literal: And he brought them to the territory of his holiness, this mountain which his right hand acquired.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he brought them in, to the border of his holy ground, to this mountain, the one his own right hand had won.
verses.directors_commentary:
‘Territory of his holiness’ is deliberately open. Radak, Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra (in his second reading) read it as the land of Israel; Ibn Ezra’s first reading and the tradition after him take it as Jerusalem, and Radak and Meiri take ‘this mountain’ as the Temple. The demonstrative זֶה, ‘this’, is the key: the psalm is sung at a place where one can point at the hill, and Ibn Ezra and Radak ask when it was said. The actor should point.

קָנְתָה is a feminine verb, agreeing with ‘right hand’ (יָמִין is feminine), not with ‘mountain’; ‘acquired’ is the verb of purchase or of creating (Exodus 15:16, ‘the people you acquired’), and the right hand is the hand of victory. The KJV’s ‘purchased’ makes it a bargain, where a conquest is meant. The verse closes the exodus journey and begins the settlement.

philological_notes.note: ‘Territory of his holiness’: the land of Israel (Radak, Metzudat David) or Jerusalem (Ibn Ezra’s first reading).
To acquire, buy or create; the verb is feminine because ‘right hand’ is. Radak glosses it as ‘established’ with a verse (‘your hands established’).

verses.translation_literal: And he drove out nations from before them, and made them fall by a line of inheritance, and made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents.
verses.translation_dramatic: He drove nations out before them. He measured the land with a cord and let the lot fall, and into the tents of the dispossessed he set the tribes of Israel to dwell.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three verbs of power, then a quiet one: he drove out, he made fall, he made dwell. The tents are the point. ‘Their tents’ are the nations’ tents (Rashi: ‘of the nations’); Israel moves into homes it did not build. The nations are, by tradition, the seven of Canaan (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David).

The middle verb וַיַּפִּילֵם, ‘made them fall’, has two senses and the psalm uses the ambiguity. Metzudat David and Radak’s first reading: God made the lot fall (cf. Joshua 13:6), assigning the land by a measuring line (חֶבֶל, also a rope). Radak’s second reading: he made the nations fall by the sword. The KJV’s ‘divided them an inheritance by line’ picks the first and loses the second. Malbim separates the stages: the seven were conquered, the land divided, and Israel settled after the division.

philological_notes.note: ‘A line of inheritance’: a measuring cord used to survey and allot land. Metzudat Zion: ‘the measuring line’.
Hiphil of ‘fall’: ‘he made them fall’, by lot (Metzudat David, Radak) or by the sword (Radak’s other reading).

verses.translation_literal: And they tested and rebelled against God Most High, and his testimonies they did not keep.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet they put him to the test and defied God Most High; and his testimonies they never kept.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn comes with a flat ‘and’, without ‘but’: after all that, the people do what they did in the wilderness. Both verbs are from earlier in the psalm: וַיְנַסּוּ, ‘they tested’ (verse 18, ‘they tested God in their heart’), and וַיַּמְרוּ, ‘they rebelled’ (verse 17). The psalm is now repeating its first accusation in the land; the pattern is the point.

‘God Most High’ (אֱלֹהִים עֶלְיוֹן) is the title of the highest God, as in Genesis 14:19; the rebellion is against the one above all. The KJV’s ‘tempted and provoked’ is archaic: ‘tempted’ meant ‘tested’ and ‘provoked’ is closer to ‘defied’ than to ‘irritated’, and BBE’s ‘bitter against’ is not what מָרָה means. ‘Testimonies’ (עֵדוֹת) are the covenant stipulations, the law the ark held. Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David set the time in the age of the judges, after Joshua and his elders; Ibn Ezra takes it as the beginning of the tale of Ephraim.

philological_notes.note: ‘They tested’: putting God to the proof, as at Massah; KJV ‘tempted’ is the old English sense.
To rebel, be defiant; BBE ‘bitter’ confuses it with מרר.
‘His testimonies’: the covenant stipulations, the law as witness to the relationship.

verses.translation_literal: And they turned back and acted treacherously like their fathers; they twisted like a bow of deceit.
verses.translation_dramatic: They fell back. They broke faith, as their fathers had before them, and slewed round like a crooked bow that sends the arrow wide of the mark.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image is the heart of the verse: a קֶשֶׁת רְמִיָּה, a ‘bow of deceit’. Rashi says it is a bow that does not shoot the arrow where the archer wants; Meiri explains that the strings are not true, or, in another reading, that the archer feigns a different aim to catch his target unaware. Radak and Metzudat David take the second sense and apply it to the people: they served God all the days of the judge and the moment the judge died, turned the other way (Judges 2:19). The KJV’s ‘deceitful bow’ is right but vague; it should be the archer’s sleight, or the warped weapon.

Ibn Ezra debates whether רְמִיָּה is an adjective or a noun meaning ‘archer’ (from רֹמֵי קֶשֶׁת), which is why I keep the plain ‘of deceit’. ‘Like their fathers’ points back to the wilderness generation of verse 8, ‘a stubborn and rebellious generation’. The verb וַיִּסֹּגוּ, ‘turned back’, is a retreat in battle: a people who withdraw from the line.

philological_notes.note: ‘A bow of deceit’: a bow that shoots wide, or an archer who feints one way and shoots another. Rashi gives the first, Radak and Meiri the second; Ibn Ezra debates whether רמיה is adjective or noun.
‘They turned back’: a retreat. Ibn Ezra takes it as a Niphal.

verses.translation_literal: And they made him angry with their high places, and with their carved images they made him jealous.
verses.translation_dramatic: They roused his anger with their high places; with their carved idols they stirred his jealousy.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two verbs are the vocabulary of a husband betrayed: וַיַּכְעִיסוּהוּ, ‘they made him angry’, and יַקְנִיאוּהוּ, ‘they made him jealous’, the same word as in Deuteronomy 32:21, ‘they have made me jealous with what is not god’ (Metzudat Zion). In the ancient Near East a god who is jealous is a covenant god who has been deceived, and the language is the language of marriage. The KJV’s ‘moved him to jealousy’ is acceptable but tame.

The בָּמוֹת are the open-air hilltop shrines, and the פְּסִילִים are carved wooden or stone idols, from פָּסַל, ‘to carve’. The KJV ‘graven images’ renders the second word properly. Ibn Ezra says the sin of the high places was offering to the LORD in the wrong place, not to a foreign god; Radak places it in the days of Eli and Samuel, until Samuel turned them back after the ark returned from the Philistine fields.

philological_notes.note: High places, open-air shrines. Ibn Ezra: sacrifices offered at the high places rather than at the one altar.
‘They made him jealous’; the same verb as Deut 32:21 (Metzudat Zion).

verses.translation_literal: God heard and was furious, and rejected Israel exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: God heard it, and his fury rose past all bounds; and he spurned Israel, utterly.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four short clauses, almost a gasp. ‘God heard’: the sin reaches him as a sound, which Radak reads as the words of those who worshipped foreign gods. The verb וַיִּתְעַבָּר is a reflexive of עָבַר, ‘to pass over’, which is the root of עֶבְרָה, ‘fury’, in verse 49: anger that crosses a limit. Ibn Ezra defines it as crossing the bound of anger; Malbim, as anger that crosses the line and falls on those who did not sin. The KJV ‘was wroth’ gives nothing of the verb’s motion.

וַיִּמְאַס, ‘rejected’, is the verb of refusing a thing one finds worthless; KJV’s ‘greatly abhorred’ is stronger than the root usually is, but the intensifier מְאֹד, ‘exceedingly’, is in the Hebrew. Ibn Ezra links the rejection to the destruction of Shiloh, and Radak to the exile of the ark.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael: ‘he passed over the limit’, i.e. was furious; the root of עֶבְרָה, ‘fury’, in v. 49. Ibn Ezra: ‘he crossed the bound of anger’.
To reject, spurn, refuse as worthless; the KJV ‘abhorred’ is stronger than the root.

verses.translation_literal: And he abandoned the dwelling of Shiloh, the tent he had made dwell among humankind.
verses.translation_dramatic: So he left the dwelling at Shiloh, the very tent where he had made his home among men.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the blow that the whole psalm has been walking toward: Shiloh, where the tabernacle and the ark stood through the days of the judges and of Eli, is left. ‘He abandoned’ (וַיִּטֹּשׁ) is the word for leaving a field fallow or a person forsaken. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all say that what he left was the ark, taken by the Philistines in the days of Eli (1 Samuel 4).

The wordplay is in the root שָׁכַן. מִשְׁכָּן is ‘the dwelling place’, and the second half of the line is ‘the tent he had made dwell among humankind’, so that the God who ‘dwells’ is the one who abandons the dwelling. The KJV’s ‘placed’ drops the root; he did not place it, he caused it to dwell, as in Exodus 25:8. Calling it a ‘tent’ is for the first audience a reminder that this God dwells in a tent, not in a temple; Ibn Ezra says it is called a tent because the ark stood in a house with no roof, and Radak that the ark was under curtains in Shiloh. ‘Among humankind’ (בָּאָדָם) is the Hebrew, not ‘among men’ as the KJV has it, and Malbim reads it as the place where the dwelling belonged: with people, if they were worthy.

philological_notes.note: To abandon, leave, forsake; Metzudat Zion: a word of leaving behind.
‘The dwelling of Shiloh’. The play with שִׁכֵּן, ‘he made dwell’, in the next phrase is the point.
‘Tent’. Ibn Ezra: the ark stood in a house without a roof, hence ‘tent’; Radak: it stood under curtains in Shiloh.

verses.translation_literal: And he gave to captivity his strength, and his splendor into the hand of [the] foe.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then he let go. His strength went off into captivity, and his glory fell into an enemy's hand.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hinge of the psalm: after forty verses of Israel's faithlessness, God's anger turns into an act. The 'strength' and 'splendor' are the ark of the covenant, which the Israelites carried into battle against the Philistines and lost (1 Sam 4:11). Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David all say so, and Ibn Ezra cites Ps 105:4, 'the ark of his strength'. The actors should note the grammar: the subject is God. The ark is not captured, it is given; the psalmist refuses the idea that the Philistines won on their own. The KJV 'delivered ... into captivity' is accurate, though its 'enemy's hand' flattens צָר, a word that means one who presses or constricts, a 'narrow' opponent. Hebrew parallelism gives two images for one object: strength (עֹז) and splendor (תִּפְאָרָה), the very words an ancient Near Eastern audience would use for a god's cult image, so the Philistines' seizure of the ark reads as a deity taken as war booty.

philological_notes.note: 'His strength'. The ark is called God's strength (cf. Ps 132:8, 'the ark of your strength'), so the loss is not only military but theological: the visible seat of God's power goes into captivity.
'Into captivity', a collective noun, 'the captive state' rather than a captive; usually said of people. Applied to the ark, it makes the ark a prisoner of war.

verses.translation_literal: And he shut up to the sword his people, and against his inheritance he crossed over [in wrath].
verses.translation_dramatic: He handed them over. He shut the gate on his own people and left them to the sword. And the wrath that rose in him spilled past every bank, and its target was the land and the people that were his own.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb ויסגר is "to shut up, to close in", the word for closing a door or a city gate behind someone. God does not strike here; he closes the gate and lets the sword do its work. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as "handed over", and Radak and Meiri tie it to the war in which many Israelites died. The KJV's "gave over" is fair but loses the sound of a door shutting. The same verse says "his people" and then "his inheritance", and the pairing is the point: the ones he is angry with are the ones he owns, and that makes it harder, not easier, to hear.

The last verb is התעבר, from עבר "to cross over". Angry here means passing over a boundary, anger that overflows. KJV "was wroth" and ASV flatten that image. The verb is also a pun with עברה "fury" (Rashi uses the noun on v. 63), so the sound of the two words carries the same idea.

philological_notes.note: "Shut up, close in." It pictures a gate or door closing on someone and leaving them to an enemy. Metzudat Zion glosses it "handed over" (מסר), and Radak links it to the many Israelites who died in that war.
The reflexive form of "cross over": he let his anger cross its bounds, or worked himself into a fury. The root is also behind the noun עברה, "fury". This is my own reading.

verses.translation_literal: His young men fire consumed, and his young women were not praised.
verses.translation_dramatic: Fire ate their young men. And for their daughters no one raised the wedding song.
verses.directors_commentary: The wedding is the unspoken scene. In Israelite society a young woman's honour was spoken aloud: the bridal song of praise, the הלולא (the same root as halleluyah), welcomed the bride into marriage. Here the root is passive and negated: no one praises them, because the men who would have married them are dead. Radak, Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all read it as the wedding song. 'Fire' is war itself (Radak: 'war is called fire'; Ibn Ezra compares Num 21:28), not a literal blaze. The KJV 'not given to marriage' gets the sense but loses the praise-root and the sound: the Hebrew has a long silence at the end, 'lo hulalu'. The BBE 'bride-song' comes closer. A director should stage this as an absence of music.

philological_notes.note: Pual of 'to praise', with the sense 'to be given the wedding praise'. The later word הלולא ('wedding feast') is built on it.
'Fire', a metaphor for war and for God's anger, as the Radak says; the verb 'consumed' is the usual one for fire eating and for the sword eating.

verses.translation_literal: His priests by the sword fell, and his widows did not weep.
verses.translation_dramatic: Its priests fell by the sword. And its widows could not weep.
verses.directors_commentary: The priests are Hophni and Phinehas, Eli's sons, killed at Aphek (1 Sam 4:11, so Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak). The widow who 'did not weep' is Phinehas's wife, who went into labour at the news, bore a son, named him Ichabod ('the glory has departed') and died (1 Sam 4:19-22), so says Rashi, citing the verse. The Hebrew 'will not weep' is in the imperfect tense, with the feminine plural ending -nah, a heavy, drawn-out form. Radak adds a second reading: they died of grief. Metzudat David reads that the national weeping for the ark made a widow's sorrow count for nothing. KJV 'made no lamentation' is a fair gloss; it is, however, a formal word where Hebrew has the plain 'weep'. A stage note: grief so large that it has no room for a single mourner's tears.

philological_notes.note: Imperfect, feminine plural, with the rare -nah ending: 'they could not / did not weep'. The tense lets the verse mean 'were not able to'.

verses.translation_literal: And the Lord awoke like a sleeper, like a warrior ringing out from wine.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the Lord woke, like a man shaking off sleep, like a warrior who rises roaring, and the wine falls from him.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the boldest image in the psalm: God as a drunk soldier. No other biblical writer risks it so plainly. It is not a claim that God was drunk; it is the people's feeling that he had been asleep while Israel was slaughtered, the same complaint as Ps 44:24, 'Awake! Why do you sleep, O Lord?' Radak and Metzudat David say the sleep is God's patient silence, and Meiri says it is the withdrawal of his providence. The KJV 'shouteth by reason of wine' tempers things: the verb מתרונן is a ringing cry from רנן, and the Hebrew does not say the shout is because of the wine; the warrior roars as he comes out of it (Rashi). Note that the divine name here is 'Adonai', the Lord, not YHWH, a title of the master and commander, which suits a warrior who is about to fight.

philological_notes.note: Hitpolel participle, 'shouting a ringing cry' and rousing oneself by that cry. Rashi links it to רִנָּה ('ringing cry') and takes it as the warrior stirring himself with shouting.
'Awoke', a sudden waking from deep sleep (also Ps 3:6, Gen 28:16).

verses.translation_literal: And he struck his foes backward; a reproach of perpetuity he gave to them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he struck his enemies from behind, and he laid on them a shame that time would never wear away.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Backward' (אחור) is the word the ancient reader hears with the whole body: the blow lands on the rear, the humiliating place. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Meiri, Radak and the Targum all connect it to the plague that struck the Philistines when they kept the ark: the swellings (עפלים, 1 Sam 5:6, traditionally read 'hemorrhoids' in the written text, with a polite Qere); the ark became the Philistines' shame. The Targum is explicit, 'he struck his oppressors in their rear'. KJV 'hinder parts' only half-keeps this; it is a good, old English word. The reversal is complete: Israel was struck and sent back, now the Philistines are struck and sent back. 'Reproach of perpetuity' ('olam) tells you the shame is not a passing one: the Philistines' own offering of golden tumours and mice made it a lasting monument.

philological_notes.note: 'Backward' or 'from behind'. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Meiri and the Targum read it as a hint at the tumours of 1 Sam 5-6; Radak and Metzudat David also allow that it describes Israel's foes being driven back.
A poetic, archaic form of 'to them' (Hebrew לָהֶם), common in psalms and other old verse.

verses.translation_literal: And he rejected the tent of Joseph, and the tribe of Ephraim he did not choose.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then he turned away from the tent of Joseph. He passed over the tribe of Ephraim and did not choose it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb מאס, "to reject, to spurn", is strong: it is the word for casting something aside with contempt. The KJV's "refused" is milder than the Hebrew, and BBE's "put on one side" is milder still. The verse is built as a mirror with the next one: "rejected" here against "chose" in v. 68, "Ephraim" against "Judah". Both halves say the same thing, a tent and a tribe, which is how Hebrew verse deals with one idea twice.

The "tent of Joseph" is not named, but Rashi reads it as Shiloh, which lay in Joseph's portion, and Metzudat David too: Shiloh stood in the territory of Ephraim, Joseph's son. The KJV "tabernacle" is fair but hides the plain word אהל, "tent". For a northern audience this is the sharpest line of the psalm: the place where the ark had stood is set aside, and the tribe that led the north is passed over.

philological_notes.note: "Reject, despise", stronger than "refuse". Metzudat David takes the verb to refer to the time God turned from the dwelling at Shiloh, which stood in Ephraim's inheritance.

"The tent of Joseph." Rashi says this is Shiloh, which was in Joseph's portion, and Metzudat David adds that it lay in the inheritance of Ephraim, Joseph's son. The second half of the verse, "tribe of Ephraim", repeats it.

verses.translation_literal: And he chose [obj] the tribe of Judah, [obj] Mount Zion which he loved.
verses.translation_dramatic: But he chose the tribe of Judah, and Mount Zion, the hill he loved.
verses.directors_commentary: The mirror of the verse before: where Ephraim was not 'chosen' (בחר), Judah is. The word order shifts the stress: 'chose Judah' comes after 'not chose Ephraim', placing the two lines side by side. Ibn Ezra says Judah is named because David came from it, and the whole psalm exists for his sake. The two objects each carry the marker אֶת: tribe and mountain are set down as two separate acts of choosing, not one. 'Which he loved' (אשר אהב) is rare: the psalms elsewhere say God 'loves the gates of Zion' (Ps 87:2). KJV 'the mount Zion' is accurate and clear. The BBE 'in which he had pleasure' weakens it: the verb is love. Metzudat David notes the tradition that Zion is where Isaac was bound.

philological_notes.note: 'He loved', a perfect used for a settled relation, so 'which he loves'. Zion is not only chosen for use; it is loved.

verses.translation_literal: And he built like the high [heights] his sanctuary, like the earth he founded it for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he raised his sanctuary like the heights of heaven, and set it down like the earth, founded for ever.
verses.directors_commentary: Two comparisons stand together: the sanctuary is as lofty as the sky and as firm as the ground. The first, רמים, is a bare participle, 'the high ones'. Rashi and Metzudat David take it as the heavens; Ibn Ezra and Radak supply 'high palaces' (so KJV 'high palaces'); the Targum, reading ראמים, has 'like the horn of a unicorn'. Rashi hears a pair, heaven and earth, each made by God's hands as the temple was ('the sanctuary which your hands established', Exod 15:17). 'Founded it for ever' has the verb יסד, used for laying the earth's foundations. The temple here is Solomon's, though the psalm speaks as if the mountain were all of one piece with the earth itself. Radak: unlike Gilgal, Shiloh, Nob and Gibeon, the sanctuary stays.

philological_notes.note: 'The high [things]', an adjective with no noun. Rashi: the heavens; Ibn Ezra and Radak: 'high palaces'; the Targum: 'unicorn horn'.
'He founded it', the earth's foundations as in Ps 24:2; the sanctuary shares the earth's permanence.

verses.translation_literal: And he chose David his servant, and took him from the folds of sheep.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he chose David, his servant, and lifted him out of the sheepfolds.
verses.directors_commentary: From the shrine to the king. 'Servant' (עבד) is a title of honour in the ancient Near East: a loyal vassal, a trusted minister, and the title the psalms give David again and again (Ps 89:4). The line sets the greatest throne in Israel against the humblest job: a shepherd boy in an enclosure of stone and thorn. The 'folds' (מכלאות) are the pens where the flock was shut in for the night; Metzudat Zion links the word to 'prison', a pen that holds. KJV 'sheepfolds' is correct. The verb 'took' (לקח) echoes Amos 7:15, where God 'took' the prophet 'from following the flock'. Ibn Ezra reads the verse as saying that Zion was named after David, 'the city of David'.

philological_notes.note: 'Pens', from כלא 'to shut up'. Metzudat Zion ties it to the 'house of confinement' because the sheep are shut inside. Rashi and Ibn Ezra cite Hab 3:17.

verses.translation_literal: From after nursing [ewes] he brought him, to shepherd Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance.
verses.translation_dramatic: From walking behind the ewes that still were nursing, he brought him, to shepherd Jacob, his people, and Israel, his inheritance.
verses.directors_commentary: The picture is of a shepherd who trails behind the slow ewes with lambs at the teat, setting the pace for the weak. That is his training for the throne. Radak says that the shepherd had to walk behind them to lead them slowly; the midrash that Rashi cites says that David let the kids graze on the soft tips of the grass first, then the older animals; and God said, 'He is fit to shepherd my people.' KJV 'great with young' is the weak point: the root means suckling, not pregnant. 'Jacob' and 'Israel' appear in parallel, the same people under their patriarch's two names, and 'his people ... his inheritance' recalls verse 62, where the same words stood for the people God had given over to the sword. Now the same words carry hope.

philological_notes.note: 'Nursing ewes', ewes with suckling young (cf. Isa 40:11, Gen 33:13). The root is 'to suckle', and the lamb itself is called עול.
'To shepherd', the same verb for tending a flock and ruling a people. The psalm moves from sheep to people using one verb.

verses.translation_literal: And he shepherded them according to the integrity of his heart, and with the skills of his hands he led them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he shepherded them, as the heart in him was whole. His hands knew the work, and with their skill he led them on, as a shepherd leads a flock.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on its shepherd. The first verb, וירעם, is "he shepherded them", from רעה, which means both "to tend" and "to feed". The KJV's "fed" keeps one half of it, and YLT's "ruleth" the royal half; the Hebrew has both, and the sheep image in v. 71 sets it up. תם, "integrity", is wholeness, with nothing held back or doubled. The KJV is right here.

The second half has a small strangeness: "skills" (תבונות) belong to the mind, but the verse gives them to the hands. Radak explains that the shepherd works with his hands, so understanding is said to be in them, and Metzudat David compares Jacob "guiding his hands" in Genesis 48:14. The picture is of a man who knows what to do with a staff.

The verse also closes a loop. In v. 52 God himself made his people set out like sheep and led them like a flock in the wilderness. Now, in vv. 70-72, that shepherd's task passes to David, taken from the sheepfolds. Metzudat David adds that the psalm sets David's integrity against the failures of the fathers, so that the hearers will follow him and not them.

philological_notes.note: "He shepherded them": the verb is both "to feed" and "to rule as a shepherd". Meiri and Radak read it as David acting with integrity and uprightness of heart.

"With the skills of his hands." Understanding is a matter of the mind, but here it is given to the hands. Radak says this is because the shepherd works with his hands and must lead by understanding, and Metzudat David compares Genesis 48:14, "he guided his hands" (שכל את ידיו).
